items.stem: What is aggregate demand?
options: Total planned spending on an economy’s goods and services at each price level
items.answer: Total planned spending on an economy’s goods and services at each price level
items.markingKey: AD = C + I + G + (X − M).

items.stem: Explain why the AD curve slopes downwards from left to right.
items.answer: At a higher price level: real wealth falls so consumption falls; demand for money rises, raising interest rates and reducing borrowing; exports become less competitive and imports more attractive, so net exports fall.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each effect explained (max 3) [3]

items.stem: Explain the difference between consumption and investment as components of aggregate demand.
items.answer: Consumption is household spending on goods and services for current use; investment is firms’ spending on capital goods to produce in future.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: In Jovania: consumption $700bn, investment $150bn, government spending $200bn, exports $200bn and imports $320bn. Calculate aggregate demand.

In Loristan: consumption $600bn, investment $150bn, government spending $200bn, exports $200bn and imports $320bn. (a) Calculate aggregate demand and the share of consumption in it. (b) Investment falls by $20bn. Calculate the new AD and explain how the AD curve is affected.
items.answer: (a) AD = $830bn; consumption share 72.3%. (b) $810bn; the AD curve shifts left because spending changes at every price level.
items.markingKey: (a) AD [1]; share [1] (b) new AD [1]; shift direction and reason [1] [4]

items.stem: In Istrana: consumption $500bn, investment $150bn, government spending $250bn, exports $300bn and imports $320bn. (a) Calculate aggregate demand and the share of consumption in it. (b) Investment falls by $30bn. Calculate the new AD and explain how the AD curve is affected.
items.answer: (a) AD = $880bn; consumption share 56.8%. (b) $850bn; the AD curve shifts left because spending changes at every price level.
items.markingKey: (a) AD [1]; share [1] (b) new AD [1]; shift direction and reason [1] [4]

items.stem: Extract: In Nordavia, world oil prices rose by 40% this year. Inflation rose from 3% to 7% while real GDP growth slowed from 2.5% to 0.5%. At the same time, the government has announced a large programme of training and infrastructure investment, and consumer confidence has fallen. (a) Calculate the change in the inflation rate in percentage points. (b) Explain how the training and infrastructure programme could affect both AD and LRAS.
items.answer: (a) 4 percentage points (b) G raises AD in the short run; better skills and infrastructure shift LRAS right in the long run.
items.markingKey: (a) Credit: 4 percentage points [1] (b) Credit: G raises AD in the short run; better skills and infrastructure shift LRAS right in the long run. [3]

items.stem: Extract: In Sundara, world oil prices rose by 60% this year. Inflation rose from 2% to 6% while real GDP growth slowed from 3% to 0.5%. At the same time, the government has announced a large programme of training and infrastructure investment, and consumer confidence has fallen. (a) Using an AD/AS diagram, explain how the rise in oil prices could cause both higher inflation and slower growth. (b) Explain the likely effect of the fall in consumer confidence on aggregate demand.
items.answer: (a) SRAS shifts left: higher price level and lower real output. (b) Consumption falls; AD shifts left; lower output, less inflationary pressure.
items.markingKey: (a) Credit: SRAS shifts left: higher price level and lower real output. [3] (b) Credit: Consumption falls; AD shifts left; lower output, less inflationary pressure. [2]

items.stem: Which is the formula for aggregate demand?
items.answer: C + I + G + (X − M)
items.markingKey: Components.

items.stem: In Kestria: consumption $500bn, investment $120bn, government spending $150bn, exports $250bn and imports $320bn. Calculate aggregate demand.
Which would shift the AD curve to the right?
options: A rise in the price level
items.answer: A cut in interest rates
items.markingKey: Higher C and I.

items.stem: Explain two factors that could cause aggregate demand to increase.
items.answer: Lower interest rates (C and I rise); higher consumer/business confidence; expansionary fiscal policy (higher G, lower taxes); currency depreciation (net exports); higher incomes abroad; wealth effects.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each factor, 1 mark each explained [4]

items.stem: Unemployment in Dravonia is rising and households fear for their jobs. Explain the likely effect on aggregate demand.
items.answer: Lower confidence reduces consumption and raises precautionary saving; firms invest less; AD shifts left.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: C/I fall; 1 mark: AD left [2]

items.stem: House prices in Pelora rise strongly, making households feel wealthier. What is the effect on the aggregate demand curve?
items.answer: AD shifts right
items.markingKey: AD shifts right: wealth effect raises consumption.

items.stem: The general price level in Halvoria rises. What is the effect on the aggregate demand curve? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Movement along the AD curve: a change in the price level causes a movement, not a shift.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: Movement along the AD curve; 1 mark: explanation – a change in the price level causes a movement, not a shift. [2]

At the same time, the government has announced a large programme of training and infrastructure investment, and consumer confidence has fallen. (a) Calculate the change in the inflation rate in percentage points. (b) Explain how the training and infrastructure programme could affect both AD and LRAS.
items.answer: (a) 4 percentage points (b) G raises AD in the short run; better skills and infrastructure shift LRAS right in the long run.
items.markingKey: (a) Credit: 4 percentage points [1] (b) Credit: G raises AD in the short run; better skills and infrastructure shift LRAS right in the long run. [3]

items.stem: Unemployment in Westaria is rising and households fear for their jobs. Explain the likely effect on aggregate demand.
items.answer: Lower confidence reduces consumption and raises precautionary saving; firms invest less; AD shifts left.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: C/I fall; 1 mark: AD left [2]

items.stem: What is aggregate supply?
options: The total output that producers in an economy are willing and able to supply at each price level
items.answer: The total output that producers in an economy are willing and able to supply at each price level
items.markingKey: AS: total planned output.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a shift in SRAS and a shift in LRAS.
items.answer: SRAS shifts with changes in costs of production (wages, raw materials, taxes); LRAS shifts with changes in the quantity or quality of factors of production or technology, i.e. productive capacity.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Explain why the Keynesian LRAS curve becomes vertical at full employment.
items.answer: At full employment all resources are used, so output cannot rise further; extra demand only raises prices.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: full capacity; 1 mark: only prices rise [2]

items.stem: The currency of Lunaria appreciates, making imported raw materials cheaper. What is the effect on aggregate supply?
items.answer: SRAS shifts right
items.markingKey: SRAS shifts right: lower import costs.

items.stem: A new technology raises productivity across Istrana’s factories. What is the effect on aggregate supply? Explain your answer.
items.answer: LRAS shifts right: productive capacity increases.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: LRAS shifts right; 1 mark: explanation – productive capacity increases. [2]

items.stem: For each event, state the effect on aggregate supply and explain. (i) The government of Fendaria invests heavily in education and training. (ii) The government of Fendaria raises indirect taxes on fuel used by firms.
items.answer: (i) LRAS shifts right (ii) SRAS shifts left
items.markingKey: (i) LRAS shifts right – the quality of labour and productive capacity rise. [2] (ii) SRAS shifts left – higher costs of production. [2] Total [4]

items.answer: Costs of production rise for firms using these inputs, so they supply less at each price level: SRAS shifts left.

items.stem: Where is macroeconomic equilibrium?
options: Where aggregate demand equals aggregate supply
items.answer: Where aggregate demand equals aggregate supply
items.markingKey: AD = AS.

items.stem: Explain, with the help of an AD/AS diagram, why the effect of an increase in AD depends on the level of spare capacity.
items.answer: With spare capacity (flat AS), output rises with little inflation; near full employment (steep AS), output rises little and the price level rises a lot.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: spare capacity case; 1 mark: near-capacity case; 1 mark: diagram reference [3]

items.stem: Explain how a supply shock such as a sharp rise in oil prices affects real output and the price level.
items.answer: Higher costs shift SRAS left; the price level rises and real output falls; unemployment may rise (stagflation).
items.markingKey: 1 mark: SRAS left; 1 mark: P up, Y down [2]

items.stem: SRAS shifts left because of higher oil prices. What is the likely outcome in an AD/AS model?
options: Price level rises and real output falls
Real output falls and the price level falls or rises more slowly
Real output rises with little change in the price level
Price level falls and real output rises
items.answer: Price level rises and real output falls
items.markingKey: Price level rises and real output falls: cost-push inflation and lower output (stagflation).

items.stem: AD shifts right when the economy is close to full employment. What is the likely outcome in an AD/AS model? Explain your answer.
items.answer: The price level rises with little change in real output: capacity constraints; AS is steep/vertical.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: The price level rises with little change in real output; 1 mark: explanation – capacity constraints; AS is steep/vertical. [2]

items.stem: For each change, state the likely effect on real output and the price level and explain. (i) SRAS shifts left because of higher oil prices. (ii) AD shifts right when the economy has a lot of spare capacity.
items.answer: (i) Price level rises and real output falls (ii) Real output rises with little change in the price level
items.markingKey: (i) Price level rises and real output falls – cost-push inflation and lower output (stagflation). [2] (ii) Real output rises with little change in the price level – on the flat part of AS, idle resources are used. [2] Total [4]

items.stem: Which is usually the largest component of aggregate demand?
items.answer: Consumption

items.answer: Net exports are X − M = −$50bn: spending on imports exceeds foreign spending on exports, so this component subtracts from AD.

items.answer: (a) P = 110, Y = $400bn. (b) P = 112, Y = $440bn: P +1.8%, Y +10%. (c) Both rise; the steeper the SRAS, the more of the AD increase goes into prices rather than output.
items.markingKey: (a) [2] (b) new equilibrium [1]; % changes [1] (c) slope interpretation [1] [5]

items.stem: Extract: In Selmaria, world oil prices rose by 60% this year. Inflation rose from 2.5% to 6.5% while real GDP growth slowed from 2.5% to 1%. At the same time, the government has announced a large programme of training and infrastructure investment, and consumer confidence has fallen. (a) Calculate the change in the inflation rate in percentage points. (b) Explain how the training and infrastructure programme could affect both AD and LRAS. (c) Discuss whether the government’s programme will reduce inflation in the long run.
items.answer: (a) 4 percentage points (b) G raises AD in the short run; better skills and infrastructure shift LRAS right in the long run. (c) LRAS shift lowers price pressure, but AD boost now may add to inflation; time lags; size of programme vs oil shock; judgement.
